articles.text: Tonight’s school board meeting, April 23, at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall, is likely to put in motion many impactful changes for the school, including approval for layoffs and changes to curriculum. The meeting is open to the public and can be participated in via zoom at https://us06web. zoom.us/j/84656989857. Of considerable public interest on the agenda will be the board’s recommendation for changes to music, performing arts and foreign language programs at elementary and middle school levels. The board is seeking approval of a full year of foreign language (World Languages) for 7th graders. The board also plans to recommend the following for the next school year: 60 minutes a week for 4th Grader in Theater Arts; one hour a week for 5th Graders in Arts, Band, and Orchestra. The Performing Arts Planning Committee is referring to next year as a “bridge year,” with a team using the time next year to help build a permanent plan for subsequent years. These changes will be up for board approval. “Fifth grade students will have the same number of hands-on instrumental music minutes in 5th grade that they currently have in 4th and 5th grade combined due to the amount of time required to transition, set up, and take apart instruments,” the board document states. “The class size of the instrumental music groupings will also be reduced by half; two music teachers will allow for more individualized feedback.” A presentation will be made with an update on the district’s work on Diversity Equity Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB). The work includes numerous Restorative Justice Circles at all school levels and the training of 68 students to lead group Circles. The growth of the affinity mentorship program is seen as a bright spot in the district’s work. During tomorrow’s school board meeting the district will finalize the layoffs of two veteran Human Resource Managers, Suzanne Binder and Kimberly Randlett. In the board background document, the district states they “either did not request a hearing or specifically waived their right to a hearing.” Although not on tomorrow’s agenda, community members, parents and students are likely to speak at the start of the meeting to challenge a March 27 decision by Athletic Director Tyler Small to not renew the contract of Dan Chubbock, the high school girls’ soccer coach for 17 years.

articles.text: At its meeting on Monday, April 21, Piedmont City Council approved an ordinance that will permanently close the Linda Park Off-Leash Dog Area. After listening to public comment from several impassioned residents, City Council voted unanimously to close the Off-Leash Dog Area. The Ordinance will go into effect 30 days after the decision. The topic was brought forward quickly when City Staff was contacted by the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board on February 6, regarding a citizen complaint about Linda Park’s Off-Leash Dog Area. The complaint, raising concerns about soil and animal excrement washing down the City’s storm drains, could cost the City as much as $66,000 per day in fines if it does not take action to address the Water Board’s request. articles.text: The fourth annual Piedmont Food Fest brought more than 1500 guests, and a dozen food trucks from the larger Bay Area together for an idyllic afternoon of music, food, and fun on Saturday, April 19. Sunshine greeted everyone in Piedmont Park, and the accompanying breeze made the afternoon a runaway success in bringing a bountiful multi-cultural celebration to Piedmont. Seven vastly differing musical acts and performances took the main stage in the park, requiring a schedule to get it all in. People from all over the Bay Area were able to grab all sorts of food originating from kitchens across the globe and then sit and enjoy an equally diverse array of entertainment, from acapella rap to Tahitian dance and jazz. articles.text: Editor: I have known Coach Dan Chubbock since my first year with Piedmont Soccer Club in elementary school. He is a coach who truly cares about his players and always wants them to succeed. Dan made my years on the varsity so memorable, and I will cherish the time I got to play for Piedmont High School forever. He is caring, always smiling, and makes every practice fun. He truly created the most positive girls’ high school soccer environment I’ve heard of. Dan led us to win the. North Coast Section championship in 2023 and tp second place in League the next year. He never stopped believing in us. That is why we were competitive against the state champions Archbishop Mitty and how we beat O’Dowd with a last-minute senior night goal last year. Dan has been here for 17 years. He built the competitive reputation of the girls’ soccer program. It saddens and shocks me to know he was let go without notice or discussion with the players. He is such a key part of all our communities. In no way did he deserve this. I know I will miss him, and so will the rest of the team. –Eliza Hammond
articles.title: Dan Chubbock a winning coach who cares

articles.text: Editor: Coach Dan Chubbock’s commitment and dedication have been the foundation of Piedmont High School’s girls’ soccer team’s success over the past 17 years. During my two years on varsity, he made my high school soccer experience even more meaningful and memorable than I could have imagined. He always brought positivity, laughter, and a competitive spirit that pushed us to grow and succeed. Regardless of the outcome of our games, Coach Dan had a unique ability to make us better on and off the field. It saddens me that the team culture and soccer program that Dan and many players have built over the years may not exist next year unless he is brought back. Being a part of the Piedmont High School soccer team has truly been one of my favorite parts of high school, and I am disappointed that our school felt the need to change it. Bring back Coach Dan. –Elia Kwong PHS Junior

articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department is putting on their Pop-up Putt Putt in the Park event in the Community Hall parking lot this Sunday, April 27, from noon to 4:00 p.m. Community members are welcome to play a free round of mini-golf in an all-ages course of City-created and community-created holes. Last year’s inaugural course drew more than 400 people to play mini-golf in the park and enjoy the Spring weather. This year, residents are encouraged to enjoy a picnic in the park, check out a Mobile Golf Simulator sponsored by ACE Kids Golf, and dance to music by a DJ. The 18-hole pop-up miniature golf course features a mix of holes designed by the City and the community. Community holes will be awarded with prizes for: Best overall, most creative, most clever, and best use of recycled materials. Families enjoy a mix of City-created and community-created holes at the 2024 Putt Putt in the Park. Children play at community designed courses at last year’s Putt-Putt event. An online petition with more than 300 signatures called for not closing the area, An in-person petition was presented with over 75 more signatures, and several residents voiced their concerns to the City Council. “As a taxpayer, I happily voted for the $7 million bond for schools and the $20 million bond for the pool. So not checking in and saying ‘it’ll cost this much’ just seems, frankly, rushed,” said resident David Hsu at Monday’s Council meeting. Following confirmation of the closure, Public Works staff will move forward with hydroseeding of the hillside, an erosion control measure that forms a protective shell over the soil, allowing vegetation to begin to regrow. articles.text: While you may already be familiar with small personal conservation actions, like recycling and turning off the lights, we know that sustained, lifelong action is more closely tied to individuals who see themselves as part of nature. Forging your nature identity starts with listening and observing, science skills that California Academy of Sciences educators are fostering in youth locally and nationally. Gregg Castro, cultural director for the Association of Ramaytush Ohlone in San Francisco and one of the Academy’s Indigenous partners, shares how this manifests in his community, “Native people see things in aggregate, in a network, in relationship to each other. We aren’t apart from nature, either. That’s a fundamental viewpoint that we’re working on with the Academy,” he said. “You can’t detach yourself from nature. You’re a part of it. So why don’t we just dive in, and learn what it means to be a part of that network?” The Academy’s Student Education Program is doing just that, shaping positive science identities and fostering community connections for nearly 70,000 K-5 students in San Francisco and throughout the US with hands-on field trips and interactive distance learning webinars each year. In the Academy’s backyard of Golden Gate Park one such program encourages students to listen to the environment and share what they hear. Equipped with their senses and a small bag containing the same scientific tools used by Academy biologists in their field work, the students set out. And there’s so much to observe: from the Redwoods that line their walking path to the great horned owls and coyotes regularly spotted in the nearby meadow. Academy educators encourage students to appreciate breathing in the same air as our tree “neighbors,” and highlight how humans are in relationship with nature by urging students to see humans, plants, and animals as sharing the same habitat. During hands-on exploration, students express awe, surprise, focus, and excitement upon uncovering even the most miniscule of insects, often feeling attached to the creatures they observe. Students leave the program with a new way of looking at the natural world and the knowledge that they can observe it anywhere, all they have to do is listen. Listening is highly critical in shifting your perspective and building a relationship with nature, but is often overlooked. The good news is you can start from anywhere. From April 25-28 the global community science event City Nature Challenge provides an excellent opportunity to explore and document the natural world wherever you are, from backyards to beaches and everywhere in between. Grab a friend or simply step outside with your curiosity– the natural world awaits. Solitaire Miguel us an Education Specialist with the School and Youth Programs at California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park Educator Lindzy Bivings leads an elementary school class in nature observation and exploration in the Academy’s outdoor Wander Woods classroom.

articles.text: In his final year of teaching fourth graders at Wildwood School, Martin Lewis took his students on a final field trip to explore the early California mission in Sonoma. Twenty-six students in Lewis’ class carpooled with parent chaperones to learn about California History at the mission on April 1. Lewis’s class visited General Vallejo’s house and stable to start the trip. A state park docent presented information about General Vallejo and how the Mexican government gave him 66,000 acres of land, and how he lost it all when it was taken over by Americans. The class also walked by the military barracks that Vallejo built on the way to visit Mission Solano, where a park ranger provided a tour of the chapel and told them the history of how it burned down and has been rebuilt over the years. The docent also described life as a native person working for the mission. A plaque outside the mission lists the names of people who died while working at the mission. If a name has an asterisk next to it, it was the name of a child. Lewis asked students to remember a name and write it down on a piece of paper once back in their classroom, to remember the kids. After lunch students enjoyed playing in the Sonoma Plaza. Students read the plaque of a statue in the plaza that describes the history of the bear flag and how California was once its own country for 25 days in 1846. Lewis has been teaching at Wildwood since 2007 and will retire at the end of the school year. Photos by Carolyn Pan 4th grade students explore General Vallejo’s home. articles.text: Kids will have a chance to climb up in Public Works’ trucks, complete a tree-themed art project, and possibly win a new book to take home at Piedmont’s annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration tomorrow, Thursday, April 24, from 4:00-6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The annual event, which dates back to 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. This year’s event will feature: • Public Works big trucks: Works staff uses daily in their work to keep Piedmont’s trees and public spaces healthy and beautiful. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the trucks. • Arts & crafts: Park Commissioners will be on hand to assist little ones with their creations. • Owl naming contest: A photo exhibit and naming contest will highlight raptors living in Piedmont Parks, including a nesting pair of great horned owls that have taken up residence in Dracena Park. Community members can share name suggestions online in advance at piedmont.ca.gov/ DracenaOwls. • Raffle: Kids can enter to win a Lego set or children’s book related to Arbor and Earth Day themes. New this year, a raffle for adult attendees will offer an opportunity to take home a California native plant for your garden. • Electric leaf blower demos: Gas powered leaf blowers are not allowed in Piedmont, but clean, quiet electric alternatives can get the job done. Attendees can try one for themselves at the event. The event will also include informational tables from the Piedmont Fire Department and the City’s Sustainability Division. 2025 Heritage Trees announcement The Arbor Day celebration will also feature the announcement of the current winners of the Heritage Tree designations. As many as five new trees in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces will join the 30 existing Heritage Trees. The winners will be announced at the event tomorrow. The Heritage Tree program, now in its seventh year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. This year, the City received nine nominations for Heritage Trees. articles.text: Miguel Long continued his strong senior season, winning the 2025 Del Campo Multi-Meet decathlon. Piedmont High senior Miguel Long continued his breakout season by winning the decathlon at the 2025 Del Campo Multi-Meet on Friday and Saturday, April 18-19. His score of 5,369 points topped the next-best athlete, Tim Libell of Bella Vista, by nearly 300 points. Long becomes the second PHS student to win the event after Parker Terrill won the same decathlon with a score of 5.964. Terrill went on to become the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2022. “I’ve been patiently waiting for Miggy’s hot streak to slow down but he just keeps going. He wants to get onto a great college team while also making it to the state meet, so we’re trying to find a balance between getting tons of reps and workouts in for his triple jump while also training him beyond the bare minimum for all decathlon events,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Competing in a field of 19 athletes at Del Campo, he won the long jump with a distance of 21 feet, 3 inches, won the high jump with a leap of 6 feet, .75 inches, and won the 110 meter hurdles in 16.69 seconds. Long also finished second in the 100 meter dash in 11.58 seconds, was third in the 400 in 55.36 seconds, third in the discus with a distance of 89 feet, 3 inches, and tied for third in his pole vault debut in 10 feet. He was also impressive in the shot put, placing fourth at 35 feet, 3 inches, and was fourth in the 1500 in 5:14.13. He was seventh in the javelin toss, recording a distance of 86 feet. “Training both depth and breadth when he only has so much energy and when we only get so much access to certain facilities is tough. He’s giving everything he can so we hope it all works out,” Assadi said. WACC League Meet Piedmont also competed in a WACC Meet at Mt. Eden in Hayward on Wednesday, April 16. PHS faced Alameda, winning both girls’ and boys’ meets. The boys’ team won eight events on the afternoon. Sam Shelby won the 200 in 22.84 in a field of 27 runners. Eric Venner won the 400 in 53.89 against 17 other runners. Sebastien Swain won the 3200 in 9:52.46 in a field of seven athletes. PHS’ 4x400 team of Venner, Shelby, Dean Olliphant and Maddox Ma won in 3:38.81 against two other teams. Gus Von Metzsch won the shot put with a distance of 38 feet, 4 inches against 13 athletes. Colby Hong won the discus in 105 feet in a field of 15. Long won the high jump in 6 feet 2 inches against nine others and the won the triple jump in 40 feet, .5 inches in a field of five. The girls’ squad also won eight events throughout the day. Caroline Taylor won the 1600 in a field of 13 with a time of 5:42.33. Amalia Gray won the 3200 against one other athlete, clocking a 12:34.87. Nia Kim won Miguel Long totaled 5,369 points to win the Del Campo decathlon. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team had a victorious week with consecutive wins at Witter Field, defeating Acalanes 15-4 on Tuesday, April 15 and Rancho Cotate 18-9 on Thursday, April 17. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 8-7 overall with one match left in its regular season. The Highlanders’ win over Acalanes was against a Division 2 North Coast Section foe, while Rancho Cotate plays in Division 1. The games were led by the strong performances of Peyton Watson and Friedie Schickedanz against Rancho Cotate with six goals apiece in both games. The pair often combined to win possession out of the face-off circle, accounting for nine victories on the draw. “Rancho Cotate was a signature win for the girls. Peyton Watson probably played one of her best games - Friedie set up 50-50 balls for her on the draw circle and Peyton just beat her opponent to the ball time and time again,” said PHS coach Carlton Chan. “The girls probably played their cleanest game of the year with few turnovers, patience on offense, and great defense,” explained Chan. Piedmont will travel to Miramonte in Orinda for its regular-season finale tonight, April 23. With a 4-1 league record, PHS goes into the Western Alameda County Conference tournament with the No. 2 seed and will host No. 3 Berkeley in the first round of post-season playoffs on Wednesday, April 30. The Highlanders defeated Berkeley 10-8 on March 28. With a win against Berkeley, the Highlanders will likely face arch rival Bishop O’Dowd for the league title for a second straight year on Friday, May 2. Piedmont has been designated as this year’s championship hosts. 15-4 win vs. Acalanes; 11-0 at halftime Piedmont held Acalanes scoreless in the first half and went into halftime holding a commanding 11-0 lead. With the large advantage, PHS was able to kill the clock in the third and fourth quarters, scoring three goals and one respectively. PHS established a 6-0 lead through the first quarter, includStaff Photos Peyton Watson scored six goals against Acalanes and Rancho Cotate. ing three goals by Watson, two goals by Chloe Graham, and one by Schickedanz. They added five more in the second quarter with two by Watson and three consecutive by Schickedanz before halftime. Schickedanz, Watson, and Graham scored three more in the third, while Schickedanz got Piedmont’s final goal of the game. Final stats: Watson scored six goals, won seven draws, and scooped one loose ball. Schickedanz had six goals, won five face-offs, and gathered one ground ball. Graham had three goals. Goalie Sophie Santander recorded six saves. 18-9 win over Rancho Cotate Piedmont jumped out to an 8-3 lead in the first quarter and Friedie Schickedanz also scored six goals.

articles.text: Piedmont High swimmers brought serious energy to a high-intensity meet against Berkeley, with the varsity boys sweeping every event in a 100–70 win. “Overall, the meet was exciting and fun,” said Head Coach Adrien Downey. “The team seating was a little cramped and old-school, but we had front-row seats to the action, and the cheering and energy was a lot better.” Though the varsity girls lost 105–64 and the JV boys fell 106–40, Downey emphasized the strong individual performances across the board. “Our varsity boys created a lot of momentum right out of the gate in the first relay, and sustained it by winning every single event of the meet,” Downey said. “Asher Takazawa gave us an early lead in the 200 medley relay with a lifetime best in the 50 back, then dominated the 200 IM and 100 back. Cole Carnazzo showed even more reasons why he’s one of the most versatile and reliable swimmers in the conference. His wins in the 100 fly and 500 free were not only impressive performances in themselves, but he beat Berkeley’s fastest swimmer which helped secure the team victory for us.” JV boys also impressed: “Zayd Mahmood, Dean Kvoriak, Rylan Patty, and Theo Ferguson all showed major speed improvements. They held their own against a much deeper squad.” On the girls’ side, Downey noted the team stepped up under tough circumstances. “All our girls swam varsity to cover injuries and illness, and they stayed focused. Cynthia Wu had her best meet of the year, giving us a chance in the medley relay with her excellent backstroke, plus wins in the 50 free and 100 back. Abigail Jacoby raced smart and with heart, and came back with a dominant 100 free after a tough 200 IM. Isla McCardell swam several great races, but none more exciting than her upset victory in the 100 breaststroke win.” Piedmont faces Castro Valley on Friday in their final dual meet before WACC and NCS. articles.text: Vocal performance at SF Conservatory of Music this weekend Isaac Mizrahi Fashion designer and television personality Isaac Mizrahi sings cabaret classics at SF Conservatory of Music’s Caroline H. Hume Concert Hall stage this Friday and Saturday, April 25 and 26. Mizrahi is best known for his eponymous fashion lines and for dressing Hollywood’s elite, including Nicole Kidman, Selma Blair, Julia Roberts and Sarah Jessica Parker. He hosted his own television talk show for seven years and made numerous appearances in movies and on television, most recently in Project Runway: All-Stars. articles.text: Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster, currently running at the War Memorial Opera House, presents four dynamic contemporary dance works from the oeuvre of Hans van Manen, the renowned Dutch choreographer. A modernizing force in classical ballet, Van Manen is known for his minimalist storytelling and maximal impact. Over a prolific career — he’s now 92 — Van Manen has created more than 150 ballets and worked with every major Dutch company, including Nederlands Dans Theater and Dutch National Ballet, where he remains a resident choreographer. The evening opened with Grosse Fuge, a physically demanding piece that explores gender roles and power dynamics, set to Beethoven’s stormy string quartet. Four pairs of dancers engage in a kinetic dialogue — dancing for each other, with each other, even against each other — and moving fluidly between defiance and surrender, assertion and ambiguity. The women, costumed in understated nude-colored leotards, seem to downplay the beauty traditionally associated with femininity. The men, by contrast, wear long, flaring black skirts that create a striking contrast with their bare torsos, emphasizing the force and sweep of their movements; midway through the piece, they tear them off to reveal black boxer briefs, their prominent belt buckles becoming points of visual tension, balance, and connection. After a sequence of gender-defined quartets and playful duets, the push-and-pull of attraction and rejection culminates in a sensual ensemble, each couple celebrating its presence in the world. It’s a technically demanding piece that requires not only individual precision but a deep sense of ensemble awareness. Jennifer Stahl and Max Cauthorn, Wona Park and Wei Wang, Nikisha Fogo and Aaron Robison, and Dores André and Fernando Carratalá Coloma delivered that rare combination of virtuosity and cohesion. Lighting design by Jan Hofstra was a particular delight, with a single neon line projected onto the backdrop, framing the movement in a stark, modernist glow. Photo by Chris Hardy Nikisha Fogo and Aaron Robison in van Manen’s Grosse Fuge The opening piece was followed by Variations for Two Couples, a 2012 quartet originally created for Dutch National Ballet’s 50th anniversary. Set to music by Benjamin Britten and others, the ballet continues Van Manen’s exploration of human connection, where choreographic focus is on relationship nuance. Frances Chung and Joseph Walsh danced alongside Jennifer Stahl and Adrian Zeisel, offering a compelling performance marked by a refined understanding of space and musicality. Classical lines gave way to idiosyncratic gestures—head bobs, prowling—that earned laughter from the audience. The beauty of abstract storytelling lies in its openness: we’re invited to write our own narratives, guided but never dictated by the choreographer’s intent. The third piece, Solo, offered a playful reprieve for those craving something more concrete. Set to the music of Bach, it’s a tightly structured work full of humor, energy, 0and rapid-fire exchanges. Cavan Conley, Victor Prigent, and Alexis Francisco Valdes tackled its virtuosic demands with style and wit. Dressed in slouchy purple shirts and grey tights, they bounded through cascades of pirouettes and lunges, their athleticism matched by an easy charm. The audience, clearly engaged, responded with spontaneous applause mid-phrase—a testament to the piece’s infectious spirit and the dancers’ crisp delivery. It was the perfect lead-up to the evening’s finale. 5 Tangos, the program’s final piece, was inspired by Van Manen’s visit to a flamenco performance in Madrid. Set to the music of Astor Piazzolla, it premiered in 1977 and hasn’t lost a bit of its edge. Dancers in bold red-and-black costumes set the tone immediately: drama, elegance, fire. A staple of contemporary ballet repertoires worldwide, 5 Tangos is both a crowd-pleaser and a masterpiece. Pointe shoes replace tango heels; Spanish inflections in Piazzolla’s score blend seamlessly with ballroom accents, creating a rich musical and physical tapestry. As in all Van Manen’s choreography, the emphasis is on movement — on the beauty of line, gesture, and spatial dialogue. Dores André and Esteban Hernández led the cast with elegance and intensity, while Thamires Chuvas, Kamryn Baldwin, Jihyun Choi, and their partners brought texture and variety to the ensemble. Esteban Hernández’s solo stood out as a highlight of the night: passionate, precise, and thrilling to behold. With its flair and poise, 5 Tangos brought the evening to a triumphant close, a celebration not only of Van Manen’s remarkable legacy, but of San Francisco Ballet’s depth, range, and contemporary spirit. articles.text: Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts museums of San Francisco, is currently exhibiting more than 250 personal photographs by Paul McCartney in a never-before seen collection entitled Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm through July. The exhibition includes the Beatles’ songwriter and singer personal captures as well as video clips, archival materials and more that offer a behind-the-scenes look at the meteoric rise of one of the world’s most celebrated and popular bands. Images span December 1963 through February 1964 and chronicle the Beatles’ journey to megastardom. Photographs were taken by McCartney with a single-lens reflex camera, which were introduced in the 1950’s as part of a new generation of handheld cameras. Sally Martin Katz, Legion of Honor Assistant Curator of Photography, said that McCartney acquired the camera in 1963 at a time “when many were experimenting with this newly popularized medium.” “The technology of the 35mm handheld camera allowed for a spontaneity in picture-taking, leading to the emergence of a snapshot aesthetic that embraced imperfection,” Katz said. “McCartney’s pictures reflect this new spirit in photography, as well as the literal blur of travel that The Beatles were experiencing, rapidly moving from one place to another.” Katz added that the exhibition, which includes photographs printed for the first time, captures “Beatlemania in full force.” “They depict the frenzied crowds chasing the band down the New York City streets, for example, and the swarms of people greeting them at the Miami airport,” she said. “The Beatles were at the eye of the storm they created: thousands of eyes were looking to capture that storm, and McCartney, with his camera, returned their gazes.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/paul-mccartney-photographs to learn more. articles.text: Guest speaker is former NYT Correspondent John J. Geoghegan Journalist John J. Geoghegan Treasure Island Museum welcomes former Special Correspondent for the New York Times John J. Geoghegan this Saturday, April 26, to discuss the mystery surrounding the “Ghost Blimp” that lifted off from the island in 1942 and was discovered off the shore of Ocean Beach with crew members missing. According to historical accounts, at 11:15 a.m., several hours after the airship lifted off from Treasure Island, it reappeared near Fort Funston and briefly made contact with the ground at Ocean Beach, causing damage to the airship. It then drifted over San Francisco and crashed on Bellevue Avenue in Daly City. No traces of the airship’s crewmen, Lieutenant Ernest DeWitt Cody and Ensign Charles Adams, have ever been found. Cody and Adams were declared legally dead in 1943, and theories regarding their whereabouts arose following the incident but have not been founded. Geoghegan, specializes in reporting on unusual inventions that fail in the marketplace despite being innovative, will offer findings based on research he conducted for his recent book When Giants Ruled the Sky: the Brief Reign and Tragic Demise of the American Rigid Airship. He served as an on-camera expert for a Smithsonian Channel documentary based in part on his research for When Giants Ruled the Sky. Geoghegan also served as a guest lecturer at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business, UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business and Kansas University’s School of Journalism and Communications. In this speaker series event, he recounts the “Ghost Blimp” story using rarely seen photographs and first-person accounts to explain the mystery surrounding the airship’s wreckage. The event begins at 10:30 a.m. at the Treasure Island Museum this Saturday, April 26. Attendance is free and open to all, but registration is recommended. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/ ghost-blimp-the-enduring-mystery-of-the-l-8 to learn more and register.. Treasure Island Museum

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will present its Spring Concert on Saturday, May 17, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. As part of YPSO’s 88th season, this concert marks the 36th season under the leadership of Maestro David Ramadanoff, whose dedication has shaped generations of young musicians. A native of Cleveland, Ohio, Ramadanoff studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony under Seiji Ozawa. With a distinguished career in music education, he remains deeply committed to nurturing young talent, carefully selecting programs that highlight the diversity of the orchestra’s musicianship and showcase works from a wide range of musical eras and composers. This season, YPSO’s talented ensemble of 80 musicians, ages 11 to 18, represents cities across the Bay Area, from Napa in the north to Fremont in the south. Concert details The evening will open with Mozart’s Magic Flute Overture, a piece full of brilliant energy and theatrical flair. A favorite among musicians for its precision and technical clarity, it is often performed as a test of an orchestra’s cohesion and dynamic control. For YPSO musicians, this piece has been a particular favorite this season for being both technically challenging and exhilarating to perform. YPSO will then showcase the winners of its annual Concerto Competition. This competition provides a unique opportunity for students to step into the spotlight and perform as soloists with the full orchestra. This season, three outstanding musicians earned the honor, and two of them, violinist Carolyn Ren and cellist Donghu Kim, will be featured. Carolyn Ren (violin) will perform Wieniawski’s Violin Concerto No. 2, Op. 22, Mvt. 3. a technically dazzling piece known for its playful character and virtuosic passages. Donghu Kim (cello) will perform Tchaikovsky’s Variations on a Rococo Theme, known for its wide range of colors and emotions. The concert will conclude with Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances, the composer’s final orchestral work. YPSO Annual Online Auction Fundraiser YPSO will launch its annual online auction, running from May 17–31. The goal is to raise $10,000 to support YPSO’s music education programs, scholarships, and outreach efforts, ensuring that high-quality orchestral training remains accessible to young musicians across the Bay Area. The auction will feature an exciting selection of items, including concert tickets, unique local experiences, fine dining gift certificates, musical instruments, and more. Community members are encouraged to participate and bid, directly supporting YPSO’s mission while taking home fantastic offerings. For more details, to donate an auction item, or to discuss sponsorship opportunities, please contact ypso@ypsomusic.org. Open Rehearsal As part of its tradition, YPSO invites community members to an open rehearsal on Friday, May 16 at the final dress rehearsal before the concert. Drop in anytime between 6:00 PM and 9:00 PM to experience the orchestra in action as they make final preparations for their performance. This event is open to prospective families, relatives unable to attend the concert, and teachers with young musicians interested in joining YPSO. Please register here: tinyurl.com/ypso-open-reh. Free student tickets are available for students with valid ID. Reserve tickets online at www. ypsomusic.org/events. Founded in Berkeley in 1936, YPSO is California’s oldest youth orchestra and the first independent youth orchestra in the nation. The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra.

articles.text: Amanda Peet and Dermot Mulroney in Griffin & Phoenix I recently came across Griffin & Phoenix, a film now streaming on YouTube. It looked interesting and I read the brief summary of the plot. I was familiar with the two actors, Amanda Peet, who I recalled is always memorable as is Dermot Mulroney. The film seemed interesting, and the opening scene has Griffin (Dermot Mulroney), late 30s, sitting across from a doctor who delivers a decidedly detached diagnosis: he has a constellation of cancerous lesions throughout his chest. In response to his questions, she grimly tells him that there is nothing that can be done to save his life. He has one, perhaps two years to live. Cut to Griffin sitting in a university class – the subject matter is death and dying. And it is in that lecture hall, with an uninspired professor standing at a podium, that he meets Phoenix (Amanda Peet). Suffice it to say, they meet cute. However, to go any further would be to deprive the audience of the opportunity to watch unfold what turns out to be an unexpected and moving love story carried by two superb actors. I will mention that the interaction between them is quick and well written and possesses an edge of humor and reparté that continues. Their relationship grows while exhibiting a touching chemistry. Griffin and Phoenix is extraordinary, deeply human, while never maudlin. Griffin and Phoenix. Directed by Ed Stone. Starring Amanda Peet, Dermot Mulroney, Sarah Paulson. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated PG 13. Released in 2006. Now streaming on YouTube.

articles.text: Ponyo, written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, is a visual treat, displaying a hand-drawn style that is reminiscent of early Disney, the colors vibrant while creating a soft, less delineated, yet pleasing effect. Ultimately the success of Ponyo, at least for an American audience, rests with its narrative, which is a tad convoluted, at least for younger moviegoers. At its center, the film is a love story between a young boy, Sosuke (Frankie Jonas), and a small fish, Ponyo (Noah Cyrus). When Sosuke rescues Ponyo from the sea (she is trapped in a glass jar), she falls in love with him and wills herself to become human. Her decision has countless unintended consequences, involving her father, Fujimoto (Liam Neeson), a King Neptune of sorts, and her mother, Gran Mamare (Cate Blanchett). And so the film spins off into a tsunami-like storm that results in Sosuke setting out, with Ponyo, to find his mother (Tina Fey). While Disney enthusiastically promoted Ponyo to American audiences as one more animated feature, it is, in sum, a much different film, different in tone and dialogue from the signature Disneyesque fare. In Japan, animation, also known as animé, is not just the province of children. Adults are completely taken with the genre, as they are with magna, which are illustrated stories, drawn in black and white. Magna comics can look like phone books, can be lengthy serials, and are read intensely by a broad spectrum of Japanese society. It is likely that Miyazaki had two audiences in mind when he wrote and directed Ponyo, resulting in a story that seems more slated for an older audience than children ages 6 to 9. Like most children’s films, it does end with a moral – value loyalty, love and family above all else. But these lessons are lost in the complexity of the dialogue and the plot, tilting the narrative toward a slightly older viewing audience. Ponyo. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With voices of Noah Cyrus, Liam Neeson, Cate Blanchett. Animation by Studio Ghibli. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated G. Released in 2008. Now streaming on Fandango/prime/MAX/apple tv/Roku. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Lisa Anne Gaston died on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. Lisa Anne Gaston, a wonderful wife, mother, grandmother, teacher and friend passed peacefully on April 3, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia, surrounded by her family and a few of her closest friends. Born on an Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi, and having lived in Atlanta for the past 36 years, Lisa Anne was known for her southern charm but was a true (and emphatic) California girl at heart. She spent her childhood in Piedmont, California, where she graduated from Piedmont High School in f 1975. The only child of two pioneering physicians – Dr. Harper Gaston, a dedicated cardiologist, who founded the Kaiser Permanente Southeast Medical Group, and Dr. Anne Gaston, one of the very first female, board-certified neonatologists – Lisa Anne was raised with wit, determination and a passion for learning. She pursued her undergraduate studies at Bryn Mawr College, where she majored in political science. Her years at Bryn Mawr were some of her most treasured. She cherished the century-old traditions and made lifelong friends, many of whom she remained in touch with all of her life. Never one to shy away from a challenge, she then moved to Washington D.C., earning both a Master’s Degree in Foreign Service and International Development, as well as a Juris Doctor in International Law and Legal Studies at Georgetown University. Lisa Anne’s professional journey was as diverse as it was impressive. She began her career practicing law in New York, California and Georgia. Once in Atlanta, she transitioned into television, where she became Vice President of Public Affairs at Turner Broadcasting. Her work creating “Interact Atlanta” earned her multiple Emmy Awards and paved the way for her eventual move to Georgia Public Broadcasting, where she was recognized as one of the “Women Making a Mark” by Atlanta Magazine. It was during her broadcasting years that she met her great love and husband of 25 years, Michael Reff. In the next chapter of her life, Lisa Anne discovered her truest calling: teaching. Earning yet another Masters Degree in Education from Agnes Scott College, she spent nine cherished years teaching English and Literature at Central Gwinnett High School. With a deep love for books and a passion for writing, she inspired her students to find confidence in their writing and empowered them to discover their own voice. She loved her students, and they loved her in return. In her final days, she received an outpouring of love and gratitude from many of her past students who shared the many ways in which Lisa Anne influenced and changed the course of their lives. Lisa Anne’s life was filled with adventure and travel with her husband, Michael, and her two daughters, Allison and Hayley Harper. She was known for her radiant smile, sharp intellect, and gift for finding joy and beauty in the everyday. She never hesitated to speak her mind, stood strong in her convictions, and moved through life with an unwavering sense of self and a deep belief in angels and the power of prayer. She loved her family, her two grandsons, and her golden retrievers. The walkers met in front of the cemetery’s main mausoleum for a tour by Dennis Evanosky, a docent who has written two books on the history of the cemetery. He pointed out his “three girlfriends” right above them in mausoleum’s façade. They are statues of ancient Greek women that represent life and how well and long it is lived. Evanosky noted the last one is holding a scissors. The cemetery’s main mausoleum was built in 1928 in a neo-classical design. Five buildings were added to this central section of the cemetery through 1933, but the cemetery’s history goes much further back. In the early 1860s a group of 12 businessman led by Samuel Merritt, a San Francisco physician and mayor of Oakland from 1867 to 1869, decided the area needed a private cemetery. Two public cemeteries existed, but they were not well maintained, and the group wanted something better for their own final resting places. In 1863 they bought 200 acres of fields “well out of town,” far from the center of Oakland at a cost of $13,000, and the Mountain View Cemetery was established. Twenty-six acres were added later for its current size of 226 acres. Evanosky told the story of renowned landscape architect Fredrick Law Olmsted, who designed the cemetery in 1863. Olmsted most significantly designed New York’s Central Park, as well as much of the UC Berkeley and Stanford University campuses. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. Actually, two Fredrick Olmsteds designed the cemetery. Olmsted created the original portion and his son, “Rick,” designed a second portion further up the hill in the 1940s. There are three types of cemeteries within Mountain View, the grand, old mausoleums of early times, the monuments and headstones for more common folk, and the later in-ground plaques that make grass cutting easier. The number of people buried in the cemetery is unknown. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. Actually, two Fredrick Olmsteds designed the cemetery. Olmsted created the original portion and his son, “Rick,” designed a second portion further up the hill in the 1940s. There are three types of cemeteries within Mountain View, the grand, old mausoleums of early times, the monuments and headstones for more common folk, and the later in-ground plaques that make grass cutting easier. The number of people buried in the cemetery is unknown. In the early days, poor people 26 26 Wednesday, April 23, 2025 Features were sometimes buried in unendowed areas and a Strangers’ Plot and not recorded. People of every race are buried at Mountain View. Plots initially ranged in price from $2 to $10, and the first burial was $8 for three spots. It is estimated there are about 180,000 graves in the cemetery with room for about that many more. The group went up the main road to “Millionaires’ Row,” which was not part of Olmsted’s plan. The walkers stopped at the large mausoleum of Edson Adams, for whom Adams Point near Lake Merritt is named. Then it was up the hill to the humble grave of Julia Morgan, the architect of Hearst Castle, Chapel of the Chimes, Berkeley City Club, and many Piedmont homes. She lived from 1872 to 1957, never married, and was buried with nine others in a family plot. Her name is just one of the ten on the marker. She wanted to be “quietly tucked away with my own.” Evanosky also said the young Julia’s family was on their way to Hawaii when they stopped in Oakland, found they liked it, and decided to stay. Millionaires’ Row is a section of the grandest, most elaborate crypts that house some of the cemetery’s most famous and wealthy residents. These were successful businessmen most of whom came to California around 1850. They did not use picks and shovels during California’s gold rush to make their fortunes but rather sold the miners items needed to mine for gold. The walkers were told the histories of Charles Crocker, Domingo Ghirardelli, and others. The group stopped in front of “Borax” Smith’s mausoleum which also houses his wife, Mary, and her friend Jane Sather, who had Sather Gate built in her husband’s memory as the entrance to the UC Berkeley campus. The walkers made their way back down the hill to their cars where they expressed their thanks to Dennis Evanosky for a most enjoyable, informative tour of a beautiful place on a special day. articles.text: The Piedmont High School shield was designed in 1922. Piedmont is a small town with deep traditions. Here are three traditions that are over 50 years old. One of the long-standing traditions dates to the construction of the first Piedmont High School in 1921. The High School opened with an expected enrollment of 250 students. At the end of the first week, there were 360 students and 400 students by the end of the first semester. These students came from 14 secondary schools. In order to create a cohesive student body, the 1922 Clan-OLog – the year of the school’s first graduation class, tells us that the Rob Roy, as the school’s mascot, began in 1959. He appeared at each football game with the cheerleaders and pom-pom girls. This Scottish theme is still strong in many aspects of the school. The school’s athletic teams are called the Highlanders, sometimes Scots. T he 1924 Clan- O -Log describes the students’ thoughts on naming the first yearbook in 1922. “From the Scotch [sic], we have coined the word Clan-OThe Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling during halftime at a 1961 Piedmont football game. student body officers selected the school colors and the school motto. They also designed the school shield and created the Clan-O-Log that first year. They chose purple and white as the school colors. As noted on the High School’s website, “Royal purple symbolizes regality and suggests to all Piedmont students, the necessity of learning to rule their lives and ambitions by the mastery of their own thoughts and actions. White represents purity and suggests that true PHS students will strive to be pure in thought, speech, and act.” The student body officers then chose the school’s motto, “Achieve the Honorable,” meaning that all students demonstrate academic and personal integrity in their work. Students worked together to design the school shield with classic symbols of a winged sandal (athletic ambitions), torch (scholastic achievement), the helmet of knighthood (bravery, courtesy, honor), Minerva (patron goddess of wisdom) and the open book that shows knowledge is open to those who will learn. These were intended to address all aspects of student life. Log, Clan standing for the students and Log meaning history.” The yearbook was to be a record of all the students. The Piedmont Highlander is the student newspaper. Sweatshirts and T-shirts are printed with “Highlanders.” The Highland Fling Spring Carnival dates to 1922, and the Alpha Clan honor society began in 1924. The school’s fight song was adapted from “On, Wisconsin” with Scottish references: A Scottish Theme The students also chose a Scottish theme. Piedmont is a highland, like Scotland. The Scots were never conquered, hence the Piedmont spirit to never give up. We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Bold and bonny bunch! We eat thistles for our breakfast, Granite for our lunch, Munch, munch, munch … We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Come from Highlands brown … So fight, Piedmont, Fight till every foe is down! In the 1960s, the Scottish Highland theme was at the High School football games. Rob Roy became the official school mascot in 1959 and was on the field during all the games. At halftime, the Kiltie Band played, and the Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling. Today, the words to the fight song have been changed from “fighting Clansmen” to “fighting Scotsmen.” The yearbook name was changed from “Clan-O-Log” to “The Pride” in May 2018. Bird Calling Contest The Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest has been a beloved tradition since 1963 when a student approached biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck and asked, “Can we do something to liven things up around here?” Waxdeck gave the students an assignment to select a bird, give a report on that bird and give its authentic bird call. The raucous bird calls drew the attention of students in nearby classrooms who came to see what the noise was. What began as an exercise quickly outgrew his classroom and moved to the home economics classroom, a larger space. One year later it was moved to the school auditorium. The contest evolved into a highly competitive contest with elaborate skits and (sometimes) costumes. The top winners were flown to the Johnny Carson Show in Burbank, and later the Late Night Show with David Letterman in New York to perform their bird calls. This television exposure brought international attention to the Bird Calling Contest and to the community of Piedmont. Television performances ended when Letterman retired in 2015. Today, after 55 years, the Bird Calling Contest continues to fill the Alan Harvey Theater at the High School each spring. Years before, his El Cerrito Avenue neighborhood had been celebrating the 4th of July with their own bicycle parade, watermelon eating contest and water balloon toss. Johnson thought it was too quiet in Piedmont in the summer and expanded his neighborhood parade to a city-wide event on Highland Avenue, the main thoroughfare. Over the years the parade has grown to include bands, antique cars, floats, horse patrols, unique groups including the Balloon Platoon of tubby sailors, and the all-important neighborhood entries. Program Highlight: Piedmont Police Exploring Post Four years ago, Lucas C. joined Piedmont’s Police Exploring program with a friend. It was a decision that would alter the course of his life. Lucas became interested in Exploring after reading that it was one of very few youth programs that offered the opportunity to get involved with law enforcement. Now a senior at Piedmont High School, Lucas is preparing for college – and a career as a police officer. “Exploring has been an experience like nothing else,” Lucas says. “My friends who have completed the police academy have all said this program was the most useful thing they did to prepare. You learn how to talk to people, how to write. You learn people skills and teamwork, which are helpful even if you don’t decide to go into police work.” Lucas likes that the Piedmont Police post has him doing things out in the community like ridealongs and monitoring the Turkey Trot and the Harvest Festival. He says the program has trained him to handle himself in a range of situations from traffic stops to crime scene investigations and hostage negotiations. Lucas encourages others to consider the program as an opportunity to gain life skills. “Definitely do it!” he says. “You’ll get to see another side of law enforcement and all the effort that goes into keeping the community safe. For me, I even found my career.” Council Membership Totals 206 Cub Scouts ages 5-10 293 Scouts BSA ages 11-17 144 Venturing ages 14-20 659 Total Youth Served 16 Explorers Piedmont Police Exploring Post & Piedmont Service Club 364 Registered Volunteers
